props.title: The State of Things
props.initialSlug: When the world vanishes, survival begins.

sections.content: Wim Wenders' The State of Things brilliantly captures the death of independent filmmaking in the early 1980s. Shot in stark black and white, it follows a German crew stranded in Portugal after their sci-fi film runs out of money. The meta-commentary hits harder when you realize Wenders made this while struggling to complete Hammett (1982) for Francis Ford Coppola's Zoetrope Studios. It shares DNA with Godard's Contempt (1963) - both dissect the clash between European art cinema and Hollywood's commercial machine.

sections.content: The film's structure brilliantly mirrors its themes of creative paralysis. The first half observes the stranded crew killing time in an abandoned hotel - reading, taking Polaroids, having philosophical discussions. When producer Gordon arrives from Hollywood, it shifts into noir territory as director Friedrich tracks him through Los Angeles, leading to a devastating finale that comments on the literal death of independent cinema. The influence echoes in later films about filmmaking like Living in Oblivion (1995) and Millennium Mambo (2001).

Wenders uses the Portuguese coastal setting to extraordinary effect, with cinematographer Henri Alekan capturing crumbling buildings and violent waves that reflect the film's preoccupation with decay. These images connect to earlier Wenders works like Alice in the Cities (1974), where landscapes become characters themselves. The hotel sequences particularly recall the liminal spaces of Last Year at Marienbad (1961), though Wenders trades surrealism for documentary-like observation. SUBHEAD: The Hollywood Connection

movies.title: Wings of Desire
movies.slug: Angels watch over divided Berlin in Wenders' poetic masterpiece about love and human connection

sections.content: The Los Angeles sequences mark a radical shift, with Wenders employing noir conventions to chart Friedrich's desperate search for Gordon. These scenes prefigure the director's later American work, especially The End of Violence (1997) and Million Dollar Hotel (2000). But they also connect to a broader 1980s European art cinema trend of examining Hollywood's influence, seen in Herzog's Fitzcarraldo (1982) and Antonioni's Identification of a Woman (1982).
